title: Gupta–Newman–Rabinovich–Sinclair conjecture
formal: For every fixed finite simple graph H, is there a finite constant C_H≥1 such that, for every finite connected simple undirected H-minor-free graph G with strictly positive real edge lengths, its shortest-path metric d_G admits a map f:V(G)→ℝᵐ into some finite-dimensional ℓ₁ space satisfying d_G(u,v)≤‖f(u)−f(v)‖₁≤C_H d_G(u,v) for all vertices u,v?
definitions: H-minor-free means that deleting vertices and edges and contracting edges of G cannot produce a graph isomorphic to H, after removing loops and duplicate edges. The length of a path is the sum of its edge lengths, and d_G(u,v) is the minimum path length. In ℝᵐ, ‖x−y‖₁=Σⱼ₌₁ᵐ |xⱼ−yⱼ|. The displayed inequalities normalize the embedding to be noncontracting; permitting a common scaling factor gives the same distortion notion. The constant C_H may depend on the excluded graph H, but must be independent of |V(G)|, the edge lengths and their ratio. The target dimension m and the map f may depend on the entire weighted graph and have no computational or dimension bound. This is an existence question for all vertex pairs simultaneously. It concerns undirected shortest-path distances themselves, without a snowflake transformation, average-pair guarantee or restriction to selected terminals.
answer_criterion: Prove the displayed embedding theorem for every excluded minor H, or disprove it by finding one fixed H and weighted H-minor-free graphs whose minimum possible ℓ₁ distortion is unbounded. The exclusion parameter must stay fixed in a counterexample family. A constant-factor approximation algorithm using a stronger relaxation than the ordinary concurrent-flow LP does not by itself establish the conjecture. The planar case would be major progress but would not alone settle every H-minor-free family.
context:
The conjecture asks whether excluding a fixed graph minor removes every large-scale obstruction to representing graph distances as sums of coordinate differences. The graph can have arbitrarily many vertices and very unequal edge lengths. Its topology supplies the restriction, while the conclusion concerns the metric generated by all those lengths. Gupta, Newman, Rabinovich and Sinclair formulate this connection in their work on cuts, trees and ℓ₁ embeddings.

The target ℓ₁ space is useful because its finite metrics are nonnegative combinations of cut metrics. A cut metric assigns distance one to pairs separated by a chosen vertex subset and zero to other pairs. Coordinates can be decomposed by thresholding their values, producing precisely such cuts. Thus an ℓ₁ embedding replaces a complicated distance function by weighted separation tests that are closely connected to graph partitioning.

Trees give a concrete exact example. Root a weighted tree and assign one coordinate to each edge. For that coordinate, give a vertex the edge’s length if it lies below the edge and zero otherwise. Two vertices differ in exactly the coordinates corresponding to their unique connecting path. Their ℓ₁ distance therefore equals their original tree distance. Cycles allow competing shortest paths, which makes a common coordinate representation much harder.

The equivalent flow formulation compares two bounds on simultaneous routing. A concurrent flow routes the same fraction of every specified pair’s demand through a capacitated graph, splitting traffic among paths when useful. Every cut bounds that fraction by its available capacity divided by the demand it separates. GNRS predicts that, on any fixed-minor-free family, the best cut bound exceeds the achievable concurrent-flow value by at most a family-dependent constant, for arbitrary nonnegative demands.

Arbitrary demands are essential. Restricting to uniform demand between all vertex pairs gives an easier problem with stronger known results. Likewise, the capacity graph can be minor-free while demand pairs connect vertices in any pattern. Requiring the demands themselves to form a planar graph would change the target. The geometric formulation avoids these auxiliary conventions by requiring distance preservation for every vertex pair.

The planar case remains a central unresolved test. Rao’s general guarantee is O(√log n) distortion for n-vertex planar metrics, and Chekuri’s May 2026 lecture notes still list a constant bound as open. No growing lower bound for planar metrics is known in that account. Both a constant upper bound and a superconstant counterexample would therefore represent a substantial change in understanding.

Several restricted families do satisfy constant distortion bounds. The original work handles series-parallel graphs. Lee and Sidiropoulos prove a stronger random-tree embedding result for graphs of any fixed pathwidth k, with distortion depending only on k. Their theorem establishes GNRS for minor-closed families that exclude a tree. Fixed pathwidth is a substantial additional restriction and does not include all graphs of fixed treewidth.

This last distinction exposes a common pitfall in reading algorithmic progress. Chlamtac, Krauthgamer and Raghavendra obtain constant-factor sparsest-cut approximation on every fixed-treewidth class using the Sherali–Adams hierarchy. They explicitly explain that their stronger relaxation does not establish a constant gap for the ordinary concurrent-flow LP. Thus the inherited paper is important context and an algorithmic success, but it is not a proof of the bounded-treewidth case of GNRS.

Filtser improves a terminal-sensitive planar bound: when the terminals can be covered by γ faces of a planar drawing, their metric embeds with distortion O(√log(γ+1)). The added one simply handles the single-face case in asymptotic notation. This is constant for fixed γ and recovers the familiar n-dependent bound when all vertices require many faces. The 2024 journal-online publication refines which geometric parameter creates the loss.

There is also recent exact progress inside small planar families. Mori’s February 2026 preprint calculates the worst-over-edge-lengths distortion of K₂,ₙ as (3k−2)/(2k−1), where k=⌈n/2⌉. The values approach 3/2. This demonstrates a nontrivial bounded loss in an infinite family, rather than a counterexample with distortion growing without bound. Such examples help test the sharpness and limitations of proposed embedding mechanisms.

A solution would connect a qualitative structural restriction—excluding one fixed minor—to a uniform quantitative statement about all distances and all concurrent-routing instances. It would explain whether the logarithmic losses in current general embedding arguments are unavoidable on these graph families. The question remains meaningful independently of how efficiently the embedding can be constructed.
why: Determine whether excluded graph minors exactly prevent unbounded ℓ₁ distortion and multicommodity flow–cut gaps in proper minor-closed graph families.

importance.reason: A central link between graph minor structure, metric embeddings and the quality of the basic sparsest-cut relaxation, already open in the planar case.

progress.text: Gupta–Newman–Rabinovich–Sinclair formulate the conjecture and prove constant bounds for restricted families including series-parallel graphs; FOCS 1999 and Combinatorica 2004.
Lee–Sidiropoulos prove bounded-distortion random-tree embeddings for fixed pathwidth, establishing GNRS for minor-closed families excluding a tree.
Chlamtac–Krauthgamer–Raghavendra give a constant-factor sparsest-cut approximation on fixed-treewidth graphs using a stronger LP; this does not bound the ordinary flow–cut gap.
Filtser improves the planar terminal face-cover bound to O(√log(γ+1)); checked July 2024 revision and November 2024 online journal publication.
Mori determines the exact worst-weight distortion of each K₂,ₙ, approaching 3/2 with increasing n.
Chekuri’s updated approximation-algorithms notes still list the planar constant flow–cut-gap question as open, with O(√log n) upper bound and no superconstant lower bound.
